note: Each hypothesis names the supplied layers it uses, the physical signature it keys on, why it can catch a fault the USGS/INGENIOUS catalogue misses, and how it differs from the instruments already built in the sibling repositories.
ranking_rule: expected DTI gain = (independent evidence x expected coverage of a catalogue-missing population) / implementation cost

hypotheses.title: Basement-depth step ribbons from an independent Parker-Oldenburg inversion
layers: own inversion -> horizontal-gradient maxima + measured throw
hypotheses.physical_signature: A basin-margin or intrabasin normal fault puts a step in the basement surface. Gravity of a thin slab is proportional to its thickness, so the step appears as a ridge of the horizontal-gradient magnitude of the depth-to-basement surface. The ridge's throw (depth difference across the ridge) is the fault's displacement.
hypotheses.why_missing_from_catalogue: 80% of Nevada is covered by Cenozoic deposits and these are thicker than 1 km over about 20% of the state (Blakely & Jachens 1991). A fault under kilometre-scale fill has no surface trace to map; the catalogue is built from surface mapping, so it is blind exactly there. The catalogue reports the fault only if a younger scarp or a mapped unit contact exposes it.
hypotheses.differs_from_existing: The sibling repositories invert nothing: they use band 18 (the supplied horizontal gradient) directly, or proximity/strike statistics of the catalogue. This lane re-derives the depth surface from band 13 with the non-linear Parker series, calibrates the density contrast against GP-1012 rather than trusting the supplied slab product, and then filters candidates by MEASURED THROW -- which is what makes a lineament a fault (DD-ABOUT).
hypotheses.cost: one calibrable inversion (seconds at 400 m) + one EDT at 100 m

hypotheses.title: Concealed-step index from the throw/depth ratio (buried scarp sharpness)
hypotheses.physical_signature: The ratio of throw to the depth of burial is a proxy for whether a step is a fault plane or a depositional ramp: a fault keeps a sharp step under fill, whereas a ramp is smoothed by the same fill.
hypotheses.why_missing_from_catalogue: Same concealment argument as H-A, plus a filter that removes the drainage/topographic-artefact lineaments the older instruments emit.
hypotheses.differs_from_existing: Keys on the ratio, not the magnitude -- no sibling instrument uses an inverted-surface throw/depth ratio.
hypotheses.cost: low (one extra ratio field) but needs a truth proxy to calibrate the sharpness cut
hypotheses.blocked_on: A population of KNOWN buried faults with independently measured throws to calibrate the sharpness cut. Named free official source: USGS Quaternary Fault and Fold Database slip-rate/throw attributes (https://doi.org/10.5066/P9BCVRCK) joined to the INGENIOUS Great Basin compilation (https://doi.org/10.15121/1881483); obtainability checked, both are public downloads.

hypotheses.title: Basement-fabric (trend) blocking: steps aligned with the magnetic fabric
hypotheses.physical_signature: In the Walker Lane the basement fabric sets the fault trend. A gravity step whose azimuth agrees with the local magnetic-fabric azimuth is more likely to be a basement-cutting fault than a shallow sedimentary edge.
hypotheses.why_missing_from_catalogue: Adds a *consistency* test between two independent physics (density and magnetisation) that a surface-mapping catalogue cannot perform at all.
hypotheses.differs_from_existing: Uses the magnetic field as a fabric ORACLE for the gravity step, not as another edge detector.
hypotheses.cost: medium (structure-tensor azimuth of two gridded fields)
hypotheses.blocked_on: A second magnetic grid at a different flight-line spacing to test azimuth stability. Named free official source: USGS GeoDAWN airborne magnetic surveys, ScienceBase 657e1d85d34e23d3533209f7 / doi:10.5066/P93LGLVQ (area 2 lines 400 m apart, azimuth 90 deg, CC0) -- obtainability checked: the ScienceBase release is public, but the grids are GB-scale and cannot be fetched from this sandbox.

hypotheses.title: Isostatic-residual step under a geothermal anomaly (heat-flow guided)
hypotheses.physical_signature: A buried fault that conducts fluid shows a heat-flow or conductivity anomaly above the gravity step; requiring both raises precision without costing recall where it matters.
hypotheses.why_missing_from_catalogue: Concealment again, plus a second independent physical channel to survive the FP penalty.
hypotheses.differs_from_existing: No sibling instrument conditions a gravity step on a thermal observation.
hypotheses.blocked_on: Heat-flow / temperature-gradient point coverage inside the GeoDAWN footprint. Named free official source: SMU Geothermal Laboratory heat-flow database and the INGENIOUS Great Basin compilation (https://doi.org/10.15121/1881483, CC BY 4.0); obtainability of the in-footprint subset NOT yet verified from this sandbox.

hypotheses.title: Along-strike relief partitioning between adjacent inverted basins
hypotheses.physical_signature: Two adjacent basins whose depth maxima face each other across a narrow high are separated by an accommodation zone; a fault with opposite dip sense usually occupies it. The signature is a paired depth minimum flanking a narrow basement high at the same along-strike position.
hypotheses.why_missing_from_catalogue: Accommodation zones are usually covered by the basin fill they separate -- the classic buried transfer zone.
hypotheses.differs_from_existing: Keys on the JOINT geometry of two basins rather than on any single edge, so it cannot be reproduced by thresholding any single supplied band.
hypotheses.cost: high (paired-object matching, no supplied layer does it)
hypotheses.blocked_on: A buried accommodation zone with independent sub-surface control to test against. Named free official source: USGS/DOE geothermal well temperature logs and the GBCGE Subsurface Database (doi:10.15121/1987556); obtainability NOT yet verified here.
